primary_source.title: The Fresh Start Effect: Temporal Landmarks Motivate Aspirational Behavior

review_method: Read the version of record the authors host at https://faculty.wharton.upenn.edu/wp-content/uploads/2014/06/Dai_Fresh_Start_2014_Mgmt_Sci.pdf, the INFORMS Articles-in-Advance sheet set (print pagination is Management Science 60(10), 2563-2582). This machine has no poppler and no PDF library in the venv, so each page's Flate-compressed content stream was decompressed with zlib and its show-text operators collected in order; pages were keyed by the number printed in their own running head (even sheets print it after the title, odd sheets after the copyright line), which is why the locators below are printed pages rather than PDF indices. Note the typesetting kerns words apart ("sear ch") and renders '=' and en-dashes as octal escapes, so every quote here was read from the reconstructed sentence, not pasted from a search hit. The four datasets, the Monday result, the placebo contrast and the authors' own mechanism caveat were each located and read in full on the pages cited. Verified 2026-11-04.

claims.paraphrase: 3 field studies tracked search, gym and goal-commitment behaviour over time.
claims.support_summary: p. 4 introduces all three: "Study 1 uses daily Google searches for the term diet to examine how public interest in one particularly common aspirational activity changes over time"; "Study 2 tests whether actual engagement in an aspirational behavior (exercise) increases following temporal landmarks using university gym attendance records"; "Study 3 investigates the frequency with which people commit to a broad set of goals on the goal-setting website stickK." All three are archival field data, not a laboratory experiment.

claims.paraphrase: 66,062 commitment contracts were created by 43,012 unique stickK users.
claims.support_summary: Study 3 data, p. 11: "The data that stickK provided for this study contain 66,062 records of commitment contracts that 43,012 unique users created between October 1, 2010, and February 13, 2013 (N days = 886)." The same 43,012 users are restated in the Model table notes on p. 12. The hook's "66,062 goals" and scene 2's "43,012 people" are these two counts; the burned-in card "THE 66,062 GOALS" and the stat card name the same figure.

claims.paraphrase: Goal contracts and gym visits rose after temporal landmarks, while searches for the placebo terms news, weather, laundry and gardening did not.
claims.support_summary: p. 12: "the number of commitment contracts created is significantly higher on Mondays than on any other day of the week (all p's < 0.05 except the comparison with Tuesday)". The placebo contrast is p. 6 ("Models 2 predict search volume for the placebo terms news, weather, laundry, and gardening, respectively, using the same regression specification as Model 1") read with p. 7, where the authors report they "did not observe reliable increases following temporal landmarks in searches for any of these placebo terms—only for the term diet".

claims.paraphrase: The proposed mechanism is that landmarks open new mental accounting periods; the authors state their field data give imperfect insight into the mechanisms.
claims.support_summary: p. 2: temporal landmarks "demarcate the passage of time and open new mental accounting periods", and the two proposed processes are that markers "create discontinuities in time perceptions that make people feel disconnected from their past imperfections" and "disrupt people's focus on day-to-day minutiae, thereby promoting a big-picture view of life". The same page carries the limit the narration repeats: "it is important to acknowledge that our field data provide imperfect insights into the mechanisms responsible for the fresh start effect". Nothing in the paper measures a brain process, so no neural claim is made anywhere in this Short.

claims.paraphrase: Study 1 covered 3,104 days of US search data and Study 2 covered 5,265,104 gym person-days.
claims.support_summary: p. 4: "We downloaded data on the daily number of Google searches in the United States for the term diet over three-month intervals ranging from January 1, 2004, to June 30, 2012 (a time period including 3,104 days)." p. 8: "we create a data set that contains one observation for each gym member on each day (N person-days = 5,265,104)", with 11,912 undergraduate members reported in Table 2 on p. 9. Recorded because the dossier's experiment_design names these three datasets; no scene speaks the 3,104 or 5,265,104 figures.

editorial_suggestions.text: "You waste the week waiting to feel ready" is the channel's framing of a habit, not a finding. The paper measures when people start things, never describes anyone as wasting a week, and reports no cost of waiting.
editorial_suggestions.status: creator editorial, not a finding of Dai, Milkman & Riis (2014)

editorial_suggestions.text: "The calendar is what moved 43,012 people to start" is stated as association. The paper's own title says landmarks "motivate" aspirational behaviour and its field designs are correlational, so the video keeps the wording to what happened on the calendar rather than claiming a controlled cause.
editorial_suggestions.status: creator editorial framing of a correlational field result

editorial_suggestions.text: "The start line, not your discipline, picks when you try" is our interpretation. The paper compares days around landmarks; it never measures trait discipline or self-control capacity as a person variable.
editorial_suggestions.status: creator editorial, not a finding of Dai, Milkman & Riis (2014)

editorial_suggestions.text: The "five-second reframe" is this channel's closing device. Dai, Milkman & Riis (2014) tested no reframe, no intervention and no five-second anything, so the video offers it as a prompt and the description does not claim it works.
editorial_suggestions.status: creator editorial, not a finding of Dai, Milkman & Riis (2014)

dossier.primary_researchers: Hengchen Dai, Katherine L. Milkman & Jason Riis
dossier.institution: The Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania

primary_source.title: The Fresh Start Effect: Temporal Landmarks Motivate Aspirational Behavior

dossier.experiment_design: Three archival field studies, not a laboratory: 3,104 days of US Google search volume for the term 'diet', swipe-card gym attendance for 11,912 undergraduates (5,265,104 person-days), and 66,062 goal contracts created by 43,012 stickK users, each regressed on the days since a temporal landmark.
dossier.stat_subtitle: Archival field data (Dai, Milkman & Riis 2014, p. 11)
dossier.comparison_text: the 66,062 goal contracts clustered after landmarks, while placebo searches for laundry and news did not
dossier.broken_assumption: You tell yourself you will start when you feel ready—the calendar is what moved 43,012 people to start.
dossier.biological_mechanism: Landmarks open a new mental accounting period, filing past slips in the old one—the authors call that evidence imperfect.
dossier.real_world_tax: It is why resolutions crowd Mondays and new years: the start line, not your discipline, picks when you try.
dossier.willpower_trap: Waiting for a fresh start keeps trying scheduled; the paper documents the spike, not a better outcome.
dossier.five_second_override: The *five-second* reframe? Name the date you are actually using—tomorrow, not someday. Comment below which landmark you start on.
dossier.best_hook: You waste the week waiting to feel ready—3 field studies logged 66,062 goals, and here is what actually moved them.
dossier.loop_bridge: Because the moment a new week gets sold as a new you...
dossier.related_title: The 3 Hidden Brain Traps Destroying Your Focus
